passages.t: An old king, and a son who exalts himself
passages.happening:
“Now King David was old and well along in years, and though they covered him with blankets, he could not keep warm” (verse 1). His servants search the land for a young woman to care for him and lie by his side to keep him warm. They find Abishag of Shunem and bring her to the king. She cares for him and serves him, ‘but he had no relations with her’ (verse 4).

At that time Adonijah, David's son by Haggith, ‘began to exalt himself’, and said, “I will be king!” (verse 5). He gathers chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him. The narrator stops to add a note about the father: ‘His father had never once reprimanded him’ (verse 6).

Adonijah talks with Joab, the commander of the army, and with Abiathar the priest, and they back him. Zadok the priest, Benaiah, Nathan the prophet and David's mighty men do not (verses 7-8). Adonijah offers sacrifices and holds a feast at En-rogel, a spring just outside the city. He invites all his royal brothers and the king's officials from Judah, but not Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men, ‘or his brother Solomon’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The king who once faced a giant cannot get warm. The opening lines show how far David's strength has gone, and the question of the whole chapter follows from them: who will sit on his throne?

Bringing a young woman to an old king may also have been a test of his vigor, since in that world a king's strength was tied to his fitness to rule. The note that David had no relations with her tells the reader that his strength is gone.

Israel had no fixed rule about which son would reign. Neighboring kingdoms often favored the eldest, and Adonijah, born fourth (2 Samuel 3:4) but now the eldest living, plainly assumed the throne was his. His chariots and runners copy the display his brother Absalom put on before his revolt.

A sacrificial feast of this kind was close to a coronation banquet. Eating together sealed loyalty, and the guest list shows who was in and who was out. Joab had commanded David's army for decades, and Abiathar had been with David since his outlaw years. On the other side stand Zadok, the other chief priest; Benaiah, captain of the royal guard; Nathan the prophet; and the mighty men.

The note in verse 6 is easy to pass over. David never once corrected this son. The failures of a father, already seen with Amnon and Absalom in 2 Samuel, now spill over into a crisis about the throne.
passages.later:
Adonijah's display is his brother's: ‘Absalom provided for himself a chariot with horses and fifty men to run ahead of him’ (2 Samuel 15:1).

Behind the whole chapter stands God's promise to David: “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). The chapter asks which son that will be.
passages.hard:
What should a reader make of the way Abishag is treated?

The text tells it plainly and without comment. A young woman is chosen for her beauty and brought to an old king's bed to keep him warm. She is never asked, and she never speaks. In the next chapter her name becomes a move in a struggle for the throne (2:13-25).

The narrator neither praises what was done nor explains it away. The record shows a court in which the powerful decided what happened to her, as the ancient world often decided for young women who served kings. The Bible does not hide it. Nothing in the passage makes it right, and nothing in it is a pattern for anyone today.
passages.asks: David's strength was gone, and so, for a long time, was his attention to his son. Ask what you have left unspoken with someone you are responsible for. And ask whose voice goes unheard in the places where you hold power.

passages.happening:
Nathan goes to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. “Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, and our lord David does not know it?” (verse 11). Her life and her son's are in danger. He tells her what to say to the king, and promises to come in while she is still speaking and confirm her words (verses 12-14).

Bathsheba goes to the king's room, where Abishag is serving him, and bows. She reminds David that he swore by the LORD that Solomon would reign after him, and tells him that Adonijah has made himself king without his knowing. ‘The eyes of all Israel are upon you to tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him’ (verse 20), she says. If nothing is done, she and her son ‘will be counted as criminals’ (verse 21).

While she is still speaking, Nathan arrives and bows before the king. He asks whether David has said that Adonijah would reign, since Adonijah's guests are already eating and drinking and saying, “Long live King Adonijah!” (verse 25). He ends with a question: has the king let this happen without telling his servant who should sit on the throne after him (verse 27)?
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a court drama built on repetition and timing. Nathan scripts Bathsheba's words, she speaks them with additions of her own, and Nathan follows with his own version. The same news is pressed on the king three times, each a little sharper.

Bathsheba's fear is real. If Adonijah takes the throne, she and Solomon will be treated as traitors to it, and the next chapter shows how such rivalries could end. Nathan, the prophet who once walked into the palace and confronted David over Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12), now stands beside her for her son.

Notice who was left off Adonijah's guest list: Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah and Solomon. The feast has already drawn the lines of the struggle, and everyone at court can read them.

Bathsheba speaks of the eyes of all Israel. In a kingdom with no fixed rule of succession, the old king's word was what would settle it, and everyone was waiting for him to say it.
passages.later: Chronicles tells the choice as God's own. David says there, “He has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel” (1 Chronicles 28:5). And the LORD's word to David about this son was, “his name will be Solomon, and I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign” (1 Chronicles 22:9).
passages.hard:
Did David really promise the throne to Solomon, or did Nathan and Bathsheba press it on a confused old man?

The oath they cite is not recorded anywhere earlier, and the scene is carefully staged, so some readers suspect a palace coup dressed up as loyalty. Others answer that God had marked Solomon out from his birth, when the LORD loved him and sent Nathan to name him Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD (2 Samuel 12:24-25), and that Chronicles presents God himself as choosing Solomon. They note too that David answers with full clarity and a detailed plan, not with confusion.

The narrator does not settle it. What he makes plain is that David confirms the choice with an oath by the LORD, and that God's promise to David moves forward even though the people who brought it about were acting in a political crisis.
passages.asks: Nathan did not wait for the king to notice. Ask where you have watched a wrong unfold and assumed someone else would speak. And ask how you tell faithful courage from clever maneuvering, in yourself as well as in others.

passages.happening:
David calls Bathsheba back and swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress, I will carry out this very day exactly what I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel” (verses 29-30). Solomon will reign. Bathsheba bows to the ground: “May my lord King David live forever!” (verse 31).

Then David sends for Zadok, Nathan and Benaiah and gives his orders. They are to set Solomon on the king's own mule, take him down to Gihon, anoint him there, and blow the ram's horn. ‘For I have appointed him ruler over Israel and Judah’ (verse 35). Benaiah answers, “Amen” (verse 36), and prays that the LORD will be with Solomon and make his throne even greater than David's.

It is done exactly as ordered. ‘Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon’ (verse 39). The ram's horn sounds, and all the people shout, “Long live King Solomon!” (verse 39). They follow him up with flutes, ‘rejoicing with such a great joy that the earth was split by the sound’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Each step answers one of Adonijah's. He had chariots and runners; Solomon rides the king's own mule, a public sign that David has chosen him. Adonijah held a feast at En-rogel; Solomon is anointed at Gihon, the city's main spring in the valley below the City of David, close enough for the sound of one gathering to reach the other.

Anointing, pouring oil on the head, marked a person as set apart by God for a task. The Hebrew verb is mashach, and from it comes mashiach, anointed one, the word behind English messiah. The oil comes from the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17), and a priest and a prophet pour it. Solomon is made king as the LORD's chosen, not only as his father's favorite.

David names Solomon ruler, in Hebrew nagid, the title given to Saul and David as leaders appointed by God. And the Cherethites and Pelethites, the royal guard, probably soldiers of Cretan and Philistine origin who served David himself, escort the new king. The army's commander has backed one son, and the king's own guard stands with the other.
passages.later: The Psalms use the same court language for a king's long reign: ‘length of days, forever and ever’ (Psalm 21:4). And the ram's horn that sounded for Solomon sounds in a psalm for the LORD himself: ‘shout for joy before the LORD, the King’ (Psalm 98:6).
passages.asks: David's word, once spoken, was carried out the same day. Ask what promise you have made that is still waiting for you to keep it. And ask whether something can be both the work of human hands and the working of God's purpose, as this anointing was.

passages.t: A feast breaks up, and Adonijah at the altar
passages.happening:
Adonijah and his guests are finishing their feast when they hear the ram's horn, and Joab asks why the city is in such an uproar (verse 41). Jonathan son of Abiathar arrives with the news: ‘Our lord King David has made Solomon king’ (verse 43). He tells it all: the mule, Gihon, the anointing, Solomon seated on the royal throne, the king's servants wishing Solomon a name greater than his father's, and David bowing on his bed to worship the LORD, who has let him see a son on his throne (verses 44-48).

“At this, all the guests of Adonijah arose in terror and scattered” (verse 49). Adonijah, afraid of Solomon, goes and takes hold of the horns of the altar, and asks that Solomon swear not to kill him (verses 50-51).

Solomon answers, “If he is a man of character, not a single hair of his will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die” (verse 52). He has Adonijah brought down from the altar, and when Adonijah bows before him, Solomon says, “Go to your home” (verse 53).
passages.hearers:
The two feasts run at the same time, and the noise of one carries to the other. Jonathan's long report repeats David's orders and their fulfillment a third time, so the whole turn of events is heard again from the losing side. Even David's prayer is reported. He praises the LORD for letting him see a son on his throne, the first sign in the book that the promise of 2 Samuel 7 is being kept.

The horns of the altar were the raised corners of the altar of sacrifice. A person in danger could grasp them and ask for God's protection. The law gave that shelter to someone who had killed by accident, but not to someone who had killed on purpose, who was to be taken even from God's altar (Exodus 21:13-14). Adonijah has killed no one. He asks for mercy at the place where mercy was sought.

Solomon's answer is a condition, not a pardon. Adonijah will live if he proves worthy, and the next chapter shows how quickly the condition is tested.

God is barely mentioned in the chapter's action. Yet by its end a son of David sits on David's throne, as God had promised. The promise has moved forward through the plans of a prophet, a mother, a guard and a dying king.
passages.later: The horns of the altar were the place of atonement as well as refuge. The priest was to put blood ‘on the horns of the altar of burnt offering’ (Leviticus 4:25). A psalm longs for God's shelter not for a moment but for a life: “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life” (Psalm 27:4).
passages.asks: Adonijah ran to the altar when his plans fell apart. Ask whether you turn to God mainly when your own schemes collapse. And ask what it would mean to receive mercy as a way to live, and not only as a way out.
